narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 72.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk prediction, not a certainty, but it was strong enough to drive the rejection.

The decision was shaped mainly by your class standing. Your third-year standing was the single most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure; your first-year standing was the second most influential and also pushed toward failure. Both were at the lowest decile, while students who were accepted averaged around the sixth decile in each year. That gap in academic rank carried more weight than any other information. Your law school admission test score, 35 versus an accepted-student average of 37.18, was the third most influential factor, but in this case it leaned toward passing rather than failure. Even so, it was not enough to offset the concerns from your first- and third-year standing.

To improve a future application, focus on demonstrating stronger academic performance, especially through additional coursework or a record of improved grades, and seek advising on how to address your class-standing history. Consider retaking the admission test if you can raise your score, and apply again with evidence that the risk of bar failure has been reduced.
